articles.title: खतरे की घंटी: तेजी से गर्म हो रहा हिमालय, सदी के अंत तक बढ़ सकता है 6.71 डिग्री तापमान - Jagran

articles.full_text:
खतरे की घंटी: तेजी से गर्म हो रहा हिमालय, सदी के अंत तक बढ़ सकता है 6.71 डिग्री तापमान
एक नए अध्ययन के अनुसार, सदी के अंत तक हिमालय का औसत तापमान 6.71 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ सकता है, जिसमें पश्चिमी हिमालय सबसे तेजी से गर्म हो रहा है
समय कम है?
जानिए मुख्य बातें और खबर का सार एक नजर में
जागरण संवाददाता, देहरादून। हिमालय को एक समान जलवायु क्षेत्र मानना अब सही नहीं होगा। नए अध्ययन में पश्चिमी हिमालय को सबसे तेजी से गर्म होने वाला हिस्सा पाया गया है, जबकि मध्य हिमालय यानी मुख्यतः उत्तराखंड में भी सर्द रातें दिन की अपेक्षा तेजी से गर्म हो रही हैं।
बीआइटी मेसरा, भारतीय उष्णकटिबंधीय मौसम विज्ञान संस्थान (आइआइटीएम) पुणे और अशोका विश्वविद्यालय के विज्ञानियों के अध्ययन में वर्ष 1901-2020 के 120 वर्षों के तापमान आंकड़ों और आठ वैश्विक जलवायु माडल के विश्लेषण से यह निष्कर्ष निकाला है कि सदी के अंत तक हिमालय के औसत तापमान में 6.71 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक भी बढ़ोतरी हो सकती है। शोध को जर्नल आफ अर्थ सिस्टम साइंस में नौ जून 2026 को प्रकाशित किया गया है।
दिन का तापमान 1.19 डिग्री और रात का 0.99 डिग्री बढ़ा
शोध के अनुसार वर्ष 1901-1930 को आधार मानने पर हाल के दो दशकों तक सर्दियों में पश्चिमी, मध्य और पूर्वी हिमालय क्रमशः 1.06, 0.96 और 1.09 डिग्री सेल्सियस गर्म हो चुके थे। वसंत में पश्चिम में 1.08, जबकि मध्य और पूर्वी हिमालय में 0.83 डिग्री वृद्धि रही।
मध्य हिमालय में सर्द रातों का न्यूनतम तापमान 1.20 डिग्री, जबकि दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 0.72 डिग्री बढ़ा। पश्चिम में यह वृद्धि क्रमशः 1.23 और 0.87 डिग्री तथा वसंत में 1.25 और 0.91 डिग्री रही। पूर्वी हिमालय अपवाद रहा, जहां सर्दियों में दिन का तापमान 1.19 डिग्री और रात का 0.99 डिग्री बढ़ा।
रात का गर्म होना इसलिए गंभीर है क्योंकि ठंडी रातों में दिन में पिघली बर्फ फिर जमती है। रातें गर्म होने पर यह पुनर्जमाव घटता है और बर्फ पिघलने का समय तथा नदियों तक पानी पहुंचने का चक्र बदल सकता है। सर्दियों में कम बर्फ जमा होने से गर्मियों के लिए प्राकृतिक जल भंडार भी घटता है। बर्फ हटने पर जमीन अधिक सूर्य ऊर्जा सोखती है, जिससे गर्मी और बढ़ने तथा बची बर्फ तेजी से पिघलने का खतरा रहता है।
सबसे अधिक उत्सर्जन की स्थिति में वर्ष 2081-2100 के दौरान शुरुआती 1900 के मुकाबले पश्चिमी, मध्य और पूर्वी हिमालय की सर्दियां क्रमशः 7.18, 6.71 और 5.82 डिग्री तथा वसंत 6.91, 6.41 और 5.16 डिग्री गर्म हो सकती हैं। इसके उलट कम उत्सर्जन पर पश्चिमी हिमालय की सर्दी वृद्धि 2.55 डिग्री तक सीमित रह सकती है।
बर्फ पर भी बड़ा असर पड़ेगा
विज्ञानियों के अनुसार पश्चिमी हिमालय में वसंत की बर्फ 2040 तक 24.2 किग्रा/वर्गमीटर, 2060 तक 27.4 और सदी के अंत तक कम उत्सर्जन में 32, जबकि अधिक उत्सर्जन में 95.9 किग्रा/वर्गमीटर घट सकती है।
मध्य हिमालय में अंत तक 17.0-34.9 और पूर्वी में 5.5-11.1 किग्रा/वर्गमीटर कमी का अनुमान है। सर्दियों में पश्चिम में कमी 9.5 से 53.2 किग्रा/वर्गमीटर तक हो सकती है। यानी अधिक उत्सर्जन में वसंत की बर्फ का नुकसान कम उत्सर्जन की तुलना में करीब तीन गुना और सर्दियों में पांच गुने से अधिक हो सकता है।
हिमालय के तीनों क्षेत्रों के ग्लेशियरों और नदी प्रणालियों को किया रेखांकित
अध्ययन में तीनों क्षेत्रों के 15 हजार से अधिक ग्लेशियर और सिंधु, गंगा व ब्रह्मपुत्र नदी प्रणालियों पर असर रेखांकित किया गया है। जिन पर करीब 1.5 अरब लोग निर्भर हैं। पूर्वी हिमालय में बर्फ नुकसान कम है, लेकिन वहां ग्लेशियल झील फटने से आने वाली बाढ़ (जीएलओएफ) का जोखिम प्रमुख है और पीछे हटते ग्लेशियरों से बनी नई झीलों के कारण यह खतरा पश्चिम की ओर बढ़ सकता है।
विज्ञानियों ने क्षेत्रवार जलवायु नीति, जमीनी-सैटेलाइट निगरानी, उच्च-रिजोल्यूशन माडल, पूर्व चेतावनी प्रणाली, टिकाऊ जल प्रबंधन, सामुदायिक तैयारी और सीमा-पार सहयोग बढ़ाने की सिफारिश की है। शोध ने यह भी स्पष्ट किया कि अगले दो-तीन दशकों का रुझान माडल काफी हद तक समान दिखाते हैं, लेकिन वर्ष 2100 तक का तापमान मुख्यतः भविष्य के उत्सर्जन पर निर्भर करेगा।

articles.title: Wildfires and a summer of extreme heat mean Andy Burnham can’t stay quiet on climate any longer - The Conversation

articles.full_text:
New prime minister Andy Burnham’s to-do list just keeps growing. In many regards, he has wasted no time in setting out a vision for the government that puts clear distance between himself and his predecessor Keir Starmer. But despite this, amid a summer of record-breaking heat and devastating wildfires, he is still to say anything substantive on the climate issue.
Burnham has not articulated how this Labour government intends to achieve its climate objectives. The government’s Climate Change Committee (CCC) has repeatedly pointed out that the UK is not meeting the targets in the Climate Change Act 2008. Climate change has nonetheless demanded his attention – a Cobra meeting was recently called amid the extreme heat across the country.
But there is another issue on which Burnham has been quiet. And that is foreign policy, notably in relation to China. What might indeed be convenient, however, is that addressing one issue could help to tackle the other.
On climate policy, Burnham’s only meaningful pledge – to take a “pragmatic” approach to drilling in the North Sea – is a shift from the Labour position to stop issuing licences for exploration. And the perceived benefits of North Sea drilling remain contested – prices are set by international markets and so further exploration in the UK would be unlikely to ease the cost of living.
At the same time, the new prime minister inherits the outcomes of the government’s China audit, an evaluation of UK-China relations that has been ongoing since 2024. The previous year, the Intelligence and Security Committee described the UK’s approach to understanding the challenges presented by China as “completely inadequate”.
The audit has since informed the UK’s Strategic Defence Review, the National Security Strategy and its trade and industrial policies. At some point, Burnham will have to set out a diplomatic approach to China.
After the decline of the “golden age” between China and the UK (2015-2018), Starmer appeared to be attempting to rebuild relations. His visit to Beijing in January, the first for a UK prime minister since 2018, indicated a desire for a better trading relationship. Despite the obvious benefits, scepticism of the Communist Party of China (CPC) remains, as MPs demand a hawkish approach to any potential deal.
For the UK, strengthening ties with the world’s second largest economy and the largest producer of goods appears a no-brainer – even more so after leaving the EU single market. A comprehensive trade deal has not been forthcoming from the US, with greater tariffs on UK exports under Donald Trump.
Seeking the best terms with China, the world leader in advanced robotics, industrial machinery and mobile infrastructure, to say nothing of its cheap consumer goods, is the dilemma facing all countries now.
The political dilemma
The two policy areas unite around the technologies required to meet climate objectives. Increasingly, there is no alternative to working with China. Under what it calls the “new three” technologies of batteries, electric vehicles and solar, China now accounts for between 70% and 90% of global manufacturing.
The processing of the critical minerals and rare earth metals required for these technologies is also dominated by China. Its refining capacity accounts for upwards of 70% in many goods.
In our research, we argue that China is essentially subsiding global decarbonisation. But this is actually causing some negative outcomes for climate policy, particularly in the EU and the US. Rather than importing green technologies from China, many countries are seeking to build up tariff walls against them. Fears of becoming even more dependent on Chinese imports are prevailing over utilising green technologies that exist already to reach climate goals.
Burnham’s government faces the same dilemma over how to pursue a green transition and diplomatic relations with China. The UK, like other all nations, has four options.
1. Attempt to compete
This could be done by nationalising green technology manufacturing, diversifying supply chains, particularly critical minerals, or shaping the new iteration of green technology.
This option comes with potentially great economic opportunities, but equally there may be a high political cost due to the capital required.
2. Look to cooperate
In practice, this would entail limiting imports of Chinese green technologies through trade barriers. And then it would mean inviting investment from Chinese companies to produce these technologies domestically.
3. Surrender to China’s dominance
This means recognising that UK companies simply cannot compete. Instead, the UK would simply import clean tech goods manufactured in China.
4. Abandon the green transition
The government could simply opt to consolidate around fossil fuel industries. In some sectors, such as cars and renewable energy, clean tech companies would be opposed to this. However in others, including aviation, cement, chemical, plastics and steel, abandoning the green transition could reduce the need to invest in alternative technologies and free up capital to overhaul carbon-intensive processes.
Of these four options, we would suggest the UK abandons any idea of competing with China, but instead seeks to cooperate with it. Burnham’s government should indeed challenge China on areas such as human rights or security, but should also continue to seek closer trading relations for green technology.
How to approach China presents a political dilemma for governments across the world. Burnham, like others, cannot avoid the conclusion that to meet climate objectives he’s going to need a better relationship with China.

Fall is right around the corner, but that doesn’t mean the sticky, humid weather is letting up anytime soon. Jumping into your fall fragrance wardrobe too early can lead to a nightmare cocktail of bold scents with sweaty temps. “Fresh, clean, citrusy, and airy fragrances are ideal for a hot day,” says Frank Voelkl, master perfumer, DSM-Firmenich. “Green notes and fresh fruits work especially well, while light sensual notes can also be a great option.”
Givaudan perfumer Dana Schmitt agrees and adds that citrus and watery scents with green or minty undertones are a great option. “I also love florals in the summer—it's when the flowers are blooming, after all,” says Schmitt.
Another thing to consider is that heat and humidity can affect how a fragrance is perceived. Voelkl says perfumes can smell less strong as they evaporate more quickly in the heat. “Sweat and other body odors can also interact with a fragrance, which may alter how it smells on the skin,” he adds.
Schmitt says to avoid overly sweet fragrances or ones with dark woody notes, as they can feel overwhelming and harsh in the heat: “Those cozy, richer notes tend to work better in the winter. So, while the fragrance itself might be amazing, the context is different, and it could end up feeling a bit off-putting.”
If you’re on the hunt for the perfect perfume to wear during the dog days of summer, check out picks from the perfumers and other fragrance experts below.

articles.title: Will there be another heatwave in September? Here’s what we know - The Independent

The UK is forecast to receive it’s first “meaningful” rainfall for months, but experts have warned the wetter conditions may not last for long.
The Met Office has predicted heavy downpours and flash flooding for parts of the UK, before drier conditions return over the weekend.
It comes as this summer looks set to be the hottest on record, with temperatures hitting 38.1C in London last Thursday during the UK’s fifth heatwave of the year.
Provisional Met Office data shows that the UK’s mean temperature for meteorological summer so far is currently at 16.48C – that is 1.88C above the 1991 to 2020 average temperature. England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average.
The remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.
Persistent dry and hot weather has taken its toll on England and Wales with about 70 per cent in drought. Following a record dry July and very low levels of rain at the start of August, 27 million people are now under water-use restrictions.
But is there another dry and sunny spell looming over the UK?
What does the long range forecast say?
In a Sunday update, Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said: “I can’t promise rain for all of us through the week ahead, but in the south at least, it’s looking like the most changeable week we’ve seen here – well at least since the end of June.”
A jet stream which has been far in the north of the UK has allowed high pressure to dominate, causing the recent excessively hot conditions, Mr Morgan said.
Mr Morgan said it would travel south, meaning that low pressure will dominate, adding: “So a much more changeable and at times unsettled outlook through the middle part of the week – low pressure will dominate and slowly drift its way southwards.”
He said it would start to turn “cooler” as wind switches to a northerly direction, adding: “So as well as some rain, showers, and even thunderstorms in places, it will certainly feel considerably fresher than recent weeks in the south.”
Looking ahead, the Met Office’s long range weather forecast predicts that the changeable weather is likely to continue, with “parts of the UK seeing showers or perhaps some longer spells of rain” from Monday, 24 August to Wednesday, 2 August.
It adds: “Temperatures are more likely to be above normal than below overall, though the possibility of widespread or exceptional heat is lower than in recent weeks.”
However, towards the start of September, the mercury could climb once again.
The Met Office notes that from Wednesday 2 September to Wednesday, 16 September “temperatures are likely to be a little above average overall”, while “there is a chance that late season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south.”
Should the necessary conditions be met, this would mark the UK’s sixth heatwave this summer.
What records have been broken this summer?
The Met Office said on Thursday afternoon temperatures had reached 37.6C at Charlwood in Surrey, while at Wisley temperatures had hit 37.2C, and Kew Gardens in London had recorded a temperature of 38.1C – the highest temperature recorded in the UK this year.
A further 10 weather stations were at or above 36C, the provisional figures from the Met Office showed.
It makes 2026 the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.
Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.
It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.
For four months in a row temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.
July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.
By 15 July this year the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.

Climate innovation
Community-driven project helps older adults prepare for extreme heat
At 7 a.m., the heat is already settling in.
Mary, 78, wakes early to stay ahead of it, closing blinds and windows to keep the air inside cool. A fan hums as she pours a glass of water, leaving another nearby as a reminder.
By late morning, the apartment feels heavy and warm. The forecast reads 33 C with a warning to limit activity. She skips her grocery trip and calls her neighbour, who offers to help.
By afternoon, the heat has intensified. Mary feels tired and slightly lightheaded. Sitting by the fan with a damp cloth on her neck, she reviews her heat-safety tips and wonders if her symptoms are something more.
Mary's experience reflects the challenges many older adults face during increasingly frequent heat waves. Understanding those risks, and developing practical, community-centred solutions is the focus of the Comprehensive Approach to Enhance Older Adults’ Preparedness for Extreme Heat (COPE) project.
Led in part by SFU, COPE aims to help older adults better prepare for and respond to extreme heat. The project is part of SFU Climate Innovation, a critical research priority that supports a community-centred response to the impacts of climate change.
“Older adults are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat because of a combination of physical, social and economic factors,” says Theresa Pauly, principal investigator of COPE and Canada Research Chair in Social Relationships, Health and Aging.
Many older adults take medications that can affect hydration, circulation, sweating or the body's ability to regulate temperature, increasing their risk during heat events. Symptoms can also be difficult to recognize.
“Confusion is a common symptom of heat stroke, meaning individuals may not realize they are in danger or seek help when it is needed,” says Pauly.
Social and economic factors can further increase vulnerability. Limited financial resources may restrict access to cooling options such as air conditioning, while mobility challenges can make it harder to reach cooling centres and community services. Older adults are also more likely to live alone, increasing the risk of social isolation during extreme heat events.
COPE brings together researchers, older adults and community partners to identify barriers and develop practical solutions to heat adaptation. Through daily monitoring, focus groups and community engagement activities, the team is examining how older adults experience heat in their everyday lives and how services, programs and policies can better support them.
A defining feature of the project is its participatory approach.
“Rather than designing interventions for older adults, COPE works alongside them through workshops, focus groups and other participatory methods to ensure recommendations reflect lived experiences and community needs,” says Pauly.
"I guess the hottest places are the places without trees and so much pavement and concrete." - COPE participant
A community-informed approach
Beyond research, COPE is translating its findings into practical tools and programs that help older adults build heat resilience and stay connected.
The team has delivered more than a dozen heat preparedness workshops, both in person and online.
“Engaging with the community is a two-way exchange,” says Pauly. “We learn about the most pressing real-world challenges people face while sharing the latest research-informed knowledge and resources.”
Participants have also taken part in activities ranging from creative writing workshops to climate education sessions and a guided tour of VanDusen Botanical Garden exploring climate impacts on local tree species. COPE-Drama is a 10-week arts-based program that combines drama and climate education to build social connection, wellbeing and heat resilience.
“Arts-based programs provide an engaging and supportive environment for building heat resilience by combining creative expression with experiential learning,” says Pauly.
"This photo is a picture of our common room, which happens to be the only air-conditioned room in the building... this is where 160 people who live in this building can find relief from the heat." - COPE participant
Extreme heat is a growing global concern
The COPE project has seen a remarkable response from international counterparts. While COPE is rooted in local communities, the project is also contributing to a growing international effort to address the impacts of extreme heat on older adults.
Researchers in Canada, Hong Kong, Israel, Sweden and the United Kingdom are working together to better understand how older adults experience and manage extreme heat in their daily lives. Using smartphone-based data collection, wearable devices and photovoice methods, the team is exploring challenges such as maintaining social connections during heat events, managing health conditions and navigating barriers within homes and communities.
Interest from community organizations, local governments and policymakers highlights growing recognition that extreme heat requires coordinated responses across sectors and communities.
“There's mobility issues sometimes for seniors, or just anybody, and to get around to a cooling centre can be a challenge for sure." - COPE particpant
Last year, COPE researchers developed and distributed more than 100 copies of Smart & Sustainable Ways to Cope with Extreme Heat and Climate Challenges, a guide that outlines affordable cooling strategies, explains the signs of heat-related illness and addresses common misconceptions about coping with extreme heat.
Bringing communities together to build resilience
Beyond supporting individuals, the project is helping strengthen community responses to extreme heat by connecting researchers, older adults, community organizations, service providers and policymakers.
The initiative also highlights SFU's role as a convener of collaborative, community-engaged research.
“Community-engaged research is a priority at SFU,” says Pauly. “The university has a strong track record of partnering with community organizations, government agencies and residents to address complex societal challenges.”
As extreme heat becomes an increasingly common part of summer, COPE is helping ensure older adults are better prepared, better connected and better supported.
“A consistent theme among our participants has been a strong desire to contribute to solutions that extend beyond themselves,” says Pauly.
That collaborative approach will be on display at a free Seniors' Heat Resilience Community Forum, hosted by COPE and SFU's Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue on September 10, 2026. The event will bring together older adults, researchers, health-care professionals, community organizations and policymakers to discuss practical solutions for protecting older adults during extreme heat events.
Ultimately, the goal of COPE is to help older adults prepare for, respond to and recover from extreme heat while strengthening community resilience for everyone.

articles.title: Back to school: How to prevent heat-related illnesses in children - Loma Linda University

Back to school means a return to sports and other outdoor activities for many children, but with temperatures peaking in many areas of the country this time of year, taking part in those activities can leave kids susceptible to heat-related illnesses.
Among those worrisome illnesses are heat stroke and heat exhaustion.
Heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, heat stroke is a medical emergency. A person may show signs of confusion, have seizures, or lose consciousness. If treatment is not received quickly, the result could be permanent disability or death.
Meanwhile, heat exhaustion occurs when the body loses excessive amounts of water and salt, often due to sweating. Symptoms of heat exhaustion include headache, nausea, dizziness, and decreased urine output.
Heat exhaustion can turn into heat stroke quickly. Sometimes, in less than an hour.
Children at greater risk for heat-related illnesses
Jonathan Smits, MD, a sports medicine physician at Loma Linda University Children’s Hospital, said children are at greater risk for heat-related illnesses than healthy adults.
“Especially young children have a harder time keeping up with fluid intake and have a larger ratio of skin-to-body mass, making dehydration a higher likelihood,” Smits said.
Obesity and kids not being conditioned to the heat are other risk factors.
“Keep reminding kids about appropriate clothing, breaks, and drinking frequently. Encourage rest when not feeling well or showing any fever symptoms," Smits said.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that schools schedule heavy outdoor activities, like sports practices and exercise, during the cooler parts of the day. In addition, children should stay hydrated and avoid sugary drinks.
Smits said sports drinks can be helpful.
“For short activities all the extra sugar is not necessary, but as kids practice more, the electrolyte and carbohydrate beverages are great,” Smits said. “There are now many types of electrolyte drinks on the market providing low or zero sugar options and different flavors to meet any child's preferences.”
Heat-related illnesses can happen in any climate
Although heat-related illnesses are generally more common during extreme heat or high humidity, Smits said they can happen in any climate.
“Mild temperatures can also produce symptoms, particularly if not conditioned to that weather or the weather is significantly deviated from seasonal norms,” Smits said. “Other risk factors include dehydration, fever, scarring or burns, young age, and medications.”
What to do when heat-related illnesses strike
Both heat exhaustion and heat stroke should be treated as emergencies.
Smits recommends immediately protecting a child from further sun and heat exposure and to begin cooling with ice bags, a cold bath or getting in a pool. If possible, try to measure the child’s core temperature.
“Rectal temperatures are the most accurate and reliable,” Smits said.
Once cooling measures are initiated, a child should be transported to an emergency department with transport supervised by first responders.
Other heat-related illnesses adults should look out for
While heat stroke and heat exhaustion are on the more severe end of the spectrum of heat-related illnesses, Smits said parents should also be aware of a condition called “exertional rhabdomyolysis.”
“Though not necessarily a heat illness, when kids and adults resume intense physical activity after a period of rest, they can have profound muscle soreness and muscle breakdown,” Smits said. “When severe cramping or soreness are accompanied by body aches or dark urine, emergency evaluation is needed to ensure the kidneys are safe.”

Over 81 Killed In Rain-Related Disasters In Himachal So Far, Yellow Alert Remain In Many Districts
At least 81 people have died in direct rain related disasters while another 116 died in hazardous road accidents since June 30
Shimla: At least 81 people have lost their lives in rain-related disasters this monsoon in Himachal Pradesh, while another 116 died in road accidents. The state continues to be battered by incessant rain, with normal life being disrupted in many places. The heavy downpour has led to landslides and road accidents. In some areas, schools have been closed due to flood-like conditions.
The Meteorological Department has issued a yellow alert for heavy rain in various districts for the next 24 hours. A yellow alert was also issued for one or two places in seven districts of Hamirpur, Chamba, Kangra, Kullu, Mandi, Shimla and Solan. Light rain is also expected in some parts of Bilaspur, Una and Solan along with one or two rounds of moderate to heavy rain. No warning has been issued for Kinnaur and Lahaul-Spiti districts.
According to a report from the Himachal Pradesh State Emergency Operations Centre, 81 people have died in rain-related incidents since the monsoon season began on June 30. During this period, 116 people have died in road accidents in the state. The state suffered losses of Rs 1,001 crore as of August 19. Torrential rain and related incidents have led to the closure of 279 roads and malfunctioning of 310 transformers. Eighty-four drinking water schemes have also been affected.
On Tuesday, a landslide blocked the Chandigarh-Shimla National Highway (NH)-5 while on Wednesday, debris blocked the World Heritage Kalka-Shimla railway track between Koti and Gumman railway stations. The railway administration is planning to send trains back to Kalka from Gumman as a preventive measure.
Providing water to homes in this mountainous state during the rainy season is not easy. The Jal Shakti Department employees are trying to ensure water supply amid overflowing rivers and heavy rain.
Deputy Chief Minister Mukesh Agnihotri shared a video on a social media platform showing the employees working in difficult conditions. He wrote, “Even amidst overflowing rivers and heavy rain, the employees of the Jal Shakti Department are standing at the front lines with full alertness. Work is being carried out continuously at the Gallu Waterfall source to restore the drinking water scheme for Dharamshala city. The task is challenging due to heavy rain. The drinking water scheme has been restored by connecting it to the Naddi water project. Even in difficult circumstances, the employees of the Jal Shakti Department are engaged in serving the public."
Heavy rains are also triggering landslides at various places. Flood-like conditions prevailed in Parwanoo in Solan district, with rail traffic disrupted. A truck narrowly escaped falling into a drain on the Old Kasauli Road in Sector 5. The water flow was so strong after the rain that it swept away the culvert and soil.
Several vehicles have reportedly been stranded near Taksal gate due to the strong water flow. While no casualties have been reported, the strong water flow has left several vehicles stranded. Meanwhile, a hillside below Bahara University in Waknaghat on the Chandigarh-Shimla NH-5 has completely blocked one side of the four-lane road.
Traffic is also getting disrupted near Chakki Mor on NH-5 due to a large amount of debris and water on the road. The district administration has directed the company that constructed the four-lane road to ensure smooth operation of NH-5. Police personnel have also been deployed.
Solan Deputy Commissioner Manmohan Sharma said, "The district administration is on alert mode. The administration's priority is to keep all the roads in the district, including NH-5, open. Instructions have been issued to the concerned departments for this. During heavy rains, people should stay away from the rivers and streams. Also, if any incident occurs in the area, inform the administration immediately."
A major accident occurred on Tuesday evening when massive debris suddenly fell from a hillside at Bagnadhar mine in the Kamaru tehsil of Giripar region of Sirmaur district. The debris struck two vehicles and an excavator parked below. Three people were feared trapped under the debris. The incident caused widespread panic in the area.
Naib Tehsildar at Kamaru, Om Prakash said, "We have reached the spot with the relief and rescue team. The work of removing debris is continuing for the second consecutive day. Three people are reported to be trapped in the debris. The rescue operation remains challenging due to continuous rain.”
Life in Bagana subdivision of Una has also been disrupted because of torrential rains in the last 12 hours. The heavy downpour has triggered landslides and uprooted trees at several locations, disrupting traffic. Looking at the danger, Jatin Lall, the Chairman of the District Disaster Management Authority and Deputy Commissioner of Una, issued orders for the closure of all non-residential educational institutions in Bangana subdivision on August 19. The administration has also appealed to people to stay away from rivers, streams, and landslide-prone areas.
With Nakki Khad on Kaloha Road in Paragpur of Kangra suddenly overflowing, a car travelling towards Chandigarh got trapped in the raging water current. The passengers were rescued by the locals with considerable difficulty. The administration has appealed to the drivers not to risk crossing the Nakki Khad and other rain-fed ravines.

Monsoon fury in Himachal: 167 roads closed and 130 transformers down, yellow alert till August 21
Temperatures are likely to remain near normal over the next three to four days
Heavy monsoon rains continue to disrupt normal life in Himachal Pradesh, with 167 roads, including the Mandi-Kotli National Highway, remaining blocked across the state. Besides, 130 transformers and 222 drinking water supply schemes have been disrupted after sustaining damage during the ongoing monsoon season.
According to the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC), of the 167 blocked roads, 84, including one National Highway near Dharampur, are in Mandi district, followed by 35 in Kullu, 12 in Sirmaur, six each in Shimla, Kangra, Hamirpur and Una, four in Chamba, three in Lahaul and Spiti, and two each in Solan and Bilaspur.
Of the 130 disrupted transformers, 68 are in Lahaul and Spiti, 42 in Hamirpur, 12 in Solan, and two each in Shimla, Kullu and Kangra. Similarly, 107 drinking water schemes are affected in Hamirpur, 55 in Sirmaur, 28 in Bilaspur, 26 in Kangra, five in Shimla and one in Solan.
In Shimla, several vehicles parked along the Bhattakufar-Mehli road were damaged after a landslide near Bhattakufar. No casualties or injuries were reported. Teams of the district administration cleared the debris and restored traffic movement. Train services were also disrupted due to adverse weather conditions.
Meanwhile, the Meteorological Centre has issued yellow alerts for heavy rainfall across parts of the state till August 21. For August 20, yellow alerts have been issued for Kangra, Kullu, Mandi, Sirmaur, Una and Hamirpur districts, with heavy rain likely at isolated places. Authorities have warned of possible landslides and flash floods in vulnerable areas.
Light rainfall is expected in the remaining parts of the state. Temperatures are likely to remain near normal over the next three to four days, with no significant change in minimum or maximum temperatures.
During the past 24 hours, moderate to heavy rainfall was recorded in several areas. Dharamsala received 127.2 mm of rain, followed by Palampur (111 mm), Nahan (76 mm), Kasauli (60 mm), Bilaspur (57 mm), Una (39 mm), Mandi (33.5 mm), Shimla (32 mm), Solan (26.8 mm) and Sundernagar (19.8 mm).
Maximum temperatures recorded were 24.5°C in Shimla, 28°C in Dharamsala, 26.8°C in Manali, 26.5°C in Solan, 30.6°C in Kangra, 31.4°C in Una, 31.1°C in Sundernagar, 30°C in Bilaspur, 31.6°C in Hamirpur, 19°C in Kufri, 21.7°C in Kalpa, 27.8°C in Nahan, 21.7°C in Keylong and 27.9°C in Chamba.
The highest maximum temperature in the state was recorded in Mandi at 32.6°C, while the lowest minimum temperature was 12.1°C in Kukumseri, Lahaul and Spiti.

Red Alert: Urgent Blood Donation Needed in Alcorcón and Madrid
The Blood Transfusion Center of the Community of Madrid issues an urgent call due to low reserves in six blood types.
By Alberto Delgado Sanz
••2 min read
IA
Blood bag with a blurred background evoking medical urgency and the Comunidad de Madrid.
The Blood Transfusion Center of the Community of Madrid has activated a red alert due to low blood reserves in six blood types, issuing an urgent appeal to citizens in Alcorcón and the entire region.
The blood reserve situation in the Community of Madrid is critical, with six blood types (0+, 0-, A+, A-, AB- and B-) on red alert. The regional Transfusion Center has issued an urgent call to increase donations and reach optimal levels, as most blood types have low reserves.
Blood types AB+ and B+ are in a more favorable position with regular donations. However, the need for donations is pressing for the other groups, requiring an additional effort from the public to ensure care for patients needing transfusions for surgical procedures, hospital emergencies, or medical treatments.
The donation process, lasting approximately 20 minutes, requires donors not to be fasting or have consumed alcohol. Donors must complete a health questionnaire and undergo a brief medical examination. The actual donation takes about 10 minutes.
The Hospital Universitario Fundación Alcorcón has donation points available on Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from 8:00 AM to 3:00 PM, and on Tuesdays from 1:00 PM to 8:00 PM. During July, August, and September, the hours will be Monday to Friday from 8:00 AM to 3:00 PM.
“
"Donating saves lives. The beneficiaries of this resource are patients who require hospital emergencies, surgical interventions, or transfusions as part of their treatments."

Red alert for high temperatures: up to 44 degrees in some places
In Valencia, fire prevention measures have been activated in La Devesa, in El Saler
ValenciaThe Generalitat's Emergency Coordination Centre (CEE) has activated the red alert for high temperatures on the north and south coasts of Valencia, as well as on the north coast of Alicante. It has also activated the orange alert in the north and south interior of Valencia and in the interior and south coast of Alicante.
However, the CEE does not rule out that this episode of high temperatures will reach Castelló and extend until the last hours of Thursday, August 20. The hottest hours will be between 1:00 PM and 8:59 PM, with maximums of 42 degrees on the north coast of Alicante, 43 on the north coast of Valencia, and 44 on the south coast.
Restrictions and precautions
The autonomous secretary of Emergencies and Interior, Fernando Lasheras, warns of the prohibition of transit of people through fields, the suspension of works and tasks in forest areas, and the suspension of the festive-recreational use of fire in forest areas.
“It is also fundamental to act with the utmost responsibility and respect the generic prohibition of lighting any kind of fire in forest areas and in the forest influence zone (up to 500 meters) and the suspension of any type of authorization granted for sports circulation in forest areas,” remarked the autonomous secretary.
Likewise, due to this extraordinary meteorological situation, a series of additional restrictions are added, such as the prohibition of circulating on forest tracks and paths, with any type of vehicle, bicycle, or on foot, within the natural parks of Sierra d'*Espadà, Sierra Calderona, Xera-Sot de Xera, la Pobla de Sant Miquel, Túria, Falçs del Cabriol, forest area of the natural park of l'Albufera, Marjal de Pego-Oliva, Penyal d'Ifac, Sierra de Mariola, Font Vermella, el Montgó and Serra Gelada.
Closure of La Devesa
In the city of Valencia, CECOPAL met on August 18 to take measures, among which is the closure of La Devesa, in El Saler, until the 21st. The SideInfo system of the canons in El Saler has also been activated as a preventive measure due to the risk of fires.
Municipal cemeteries, street markets, and municipal swimming pools will also remain closed, as will the Serrans Towers, the Quart Towers, and Gulliver Park. Parks and gardens will remain open, subject to the westerly wind gusts that may occur.
